entry: Unique or novel device, method, composition, idea or process. An invention may improve a machine, product or process to increase efficiency or lower cost, or it may be an entirely new concept. An idea that is unique enough, either as a stand-alone invention or as a significant improvement over the work of others, can be [[Patent|patented]]. A granted patent gives the inventor a proprietary interest for a specific period, which can be licensed for financial gain. Patent rights apply only within the jurisdiction where the patent was obtained, and the rules vary by country. The earliest inventions include stone tools, such as the Oldowan tools, which date back around 2.9 million years. Inventions fall into three kinds: scientific-technological, sociopolitical, and humanistic or cultural. Scientific-technological examples include [[Vaccination|vaccination]], the [[Internet]] and the smartphone. Sociopolitical examples include the British [[Parliament|Parliament]], the [[United Nations]] and the [[Olympic Games]].

City in the [[Scottish Highlands]], northern [[Scotland]]. Long regarded as the de facto capital of the Highlands, Inverness is the administrative center of the Highland Council region. The River Ness flows from [[Loch Ness]] into the Moray Firth. Granted city status in 2000 as a Millennium City, it is the northernmost city in the [[United Kingdom]]. The greater Inverness area had a population of 56,969 in 2012 and 63,320 four years later. In 2024 it was ranked the happiest place to live in the United Kingdom.

Function reversing the effect of another function. In [[Mathematics|mathematics]], the inverse of a function f, written f⁻¹, exists if and only if f is injective (one-to-one). For a function f: X→Y, its inverse sends each element y in Y to the unique element x in X such that f(x) = y. For example, f(x) = 5x − 7 multiplies its input by 5 and then subtracts 7, so its inverse adds 7 to the output and divides the result by 5. The notation f⁻¹ was introduced by John Frederick William Herschel in 1813. Using [[Function composition|composition of functions]], f⁻¹(f(x)) = x for every x in the domain. The function f(x) = x² on all real numbers is not injective and has no inverse, but restricted to nonnegative reals it is invertible. The exponential function and the [[Logarithm|natural logarithm]] are inverses of each other.

Physical law of intensity inversely proportional to the square of distance from a source. The law generally applies when a force, energy or other conserved quantity spreads evenly outward from a point source in three-dimensional space, because the surface area of a sphere grows with the square of its radius. [[Newton's law of universal gravitation]] follows the law, as do electricity, [[Light|light]], [[Sound|sound]] and radiation. For [[Radar|radar]], energy returns as the inverse fourth power of range, because it spreads on both the transmitted and reflected paths. A [[Waveguide|waveguide]] limits the spreading of a signal, much as a canal confines water.

Inverses of the trigonometric functions, defined on restricted domains. They include the inverses of sine, cosine, tangent, cotangent, secant and cosecant, which yield an angle from a trigonometric ratio. The most common notation uses the prefix arc-, as in arcsin(x) and arctan(x); since 2019, ISO 80000-2 has specified only this prefix. Because none of the six trigonometric functions is one-to-one, their domains must be restricted to define inverses. The functions are widely used in [[Engineering]], [[Navigation]], [[Physics]] and [[Geometry]]. In calculus, the [[Derivative|derivative]] of arcsin(x) is 1/√(1 − x²).

Animal lacking a vertebral column, or backbone. The term is a paraphyletic grouping of all animals other than the chordate subphylum [[Vertebrate|Vertebrata]]. Most invertebrates belong to the clade Protostomia, including [[Arthropod|arthropods]], [[Mollusca|molluscs]], [[Annelid|annelids]] and flatworms. Echinoderms and tunicates are deuterostomes, while [[Cnidaria|cnidarians]] and [[Sponge|sponges]] lie outside the protostome–deuterostome split. Invertebrates make up about 97% of animal species by one estimate, and over 95% of described species according to IUCN figures. They range in size from 10 μm myxozoans to the 9–10 m colossal squid. Some animals usually called invertebrates, such as tunicates, are more closely related to vertebrates than to other invertebrates, so the term has no taxonomic significance. It remains in use as a term of convenience.

Medieval conflict between church and state over the appointment of bishops, abbots and [[Pope|popes]] (1076–1122). It began in 1076 as a power struggle between [[Pope Gregory VII]] and Henry IV, then king and later Holy Roman Emperor, and lasted nearly 50 years. Under the Concordat of Worms, agreed in 1122 by Pope Callixtus II and Emperor Henry V, bishops swore an oath of fealty to the secular monarch, who held authority "by the lance" but left selection to the church. The church invested bishops with sacred authority, symbolized by a ring and staff. In Germany, but not Italy or Burgundy, the emperor kept the right to preside over elections of abbots and bishops, and Holy Roman Emperors renounced the right to choose the pope. A shorter struggle between Pope Paschal II and [[Henry I of England|Henry I]] of England, from 1103 to 1107, ended with a similar Concordat of London.

16th-century Chinese novel of the gods-and-demons (*shenmo*) genre. Consisting of 100 chapters, it was first published in book form between 1567 and 1619, during the [[Ming dynasty]]. It is traditionally attributed to Xu Zhonglin and blends history, folklore, mythology, legend and fantasy. It is set in the decline of the Shang dynasty (1600–1046 BC) and the rise of the Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BC), and it romanticizes the overthrow of Di Xin, the last Shang ruler, by Ji Fa, who founded the Zhou dynasty. Its large cast includes gods, immortals, demons and spirits. Its title refers to the *Fengshen bang*, a list that empowers Jiang Ziya to invest the gods of Heaven. The novel is generally regarded as one of the most important works of Chinese gods-and-demons fiction, comparable to [[Journey to the West]].

Commitment of resources to something expected to gain value over time. In finance, investing aims to generate a return on the invested asset. The return may be a capital gain or loss, realized when the asset is sold, or periodic income such as dividends, interest or rental income. Investors generally expect higher returns from riskier investments, and high risk carries a chance of high losses. Traditional investments include [[Stock|stocks]], [[Bond (finance)|bonds]], cash and real estate. Alternative investments include private equity, other loans including [[Mortgage|mortgages]], commodities such as [[Gold|gold]] and [[Natural gas|natural gas]], collectables such as art and wine, and digital assets such as [[Cryptocurrency|cryptocurrency]]. Hedge funds may use derivatives, leveraged investing and short selling. Investment differs from arbitrage, which earns profit without investing capital or bearing risk. Diversification has the statistical effect of reducing overall risk.

Innermost and second smallest of the four [[Galilean moons]] of [[Jupiter]]. Slightly larger than Earth's Moon, Io is the fourth-largest natural satellite in the Solar System. With over 400 active volcanoes, it is the most geologically active object in the Solar System. Tidal heating from friction, generated as Jupiter pulls Io between [[Europa (moon)|Europa]] and [[Ganymede (moon)|Ganymede]], drives this activity. Volcanic plumes of sulfur and sulfur dioxide rise as high as 500 km above the surface. More than 100 mountains rise on its surface, some taller than [[Mount Everest]]. Unlike most outer moons, which are mostly water ice, Io is mainly silicate rock around a molten iron or iron sulfide core. It was discovered in 1610 by [[Galileo Galilei]] and named after a priestess of Hera who became one of Zeus's lovers. The Voyager spacecraft revealed it as geologically active in 1979.

Chemical element with symbol I and atomic number 53. The heaviest of the stable [[Halogen|halogens]], iodine is a semi-lustrous, nonmetallic solid under standard conditions. It melts to a deep violet liquid at 114 °C (237 °F) and boils to a violet gas at 184 °C (363 °F). French chemist Bernard Courtois discovered it in 1811 while investigating corrosion of copper vessels used to process seaweed ash for saltpeter. Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac named it two years later, after the Ancient Greek word for violet. Iodine is required for the synthesis of [[Thyroid|thyroid]] hormones, and its deficiency affects about two billion people, making it the leading preventable cause of intellectual disabilities. Chile and Japan are the dominant producers today. Radioactive isotopes of iodine treat thyroid cancer, and iodine is used as a catalyst in producing [[Acetic acid|acetic acid]]. It is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines.

Romanian military officer and dictator, 1940–44. A World War I veteran, Antonescu became chief of the General Staff and sympathized with far-right and fascist politics. In September 1940 King Carol II appointed him prime minister with dictatorial powers. He established the National Legionary State in an uneasy partnership with the Iron Guard, suppressed the Guard after its January 1941 rebellion, and aligned Romania with [[Nazi Germany]]. Romanian forces joined the invasion of the [[Soviet Union]] in June 1941 as part of [[Operation Barbarossa]], and Antonescu recovered Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina. His regime was responsible for many deaths, mostly of Jews in Bessarabia, Ukraine and Romania, and of Romanian Romani, through pogroms and deportations to Transnistria. Heavy losses on the Eastern Front led him to seek peace talks. On August 23, 1944, King Michael I led a coup; Antonescu was arrested, convicted of war crimes after the war, and executed.

Atom or molecule with a net electrical charge. The net charge is nonzero because the atom or molecule has a different number of [[Electron|electrons]] than [[Proton|protons]]. A cation is positively charged, with fewer electrons than protons, as in the [[Potassium|potassium]] ion K⁺. An anion is negatively charged, with more electrons, as in the [[Chloride|chloride]] ion Cl⁻ and the hydroxide ion OH⁻. Opposite charges attract, so cations and anions readily form [[Chemical bond|ionic compounds]]. An ion of a single atom is monatomic; one of two or more atoms is polyatomic. The term was coined by [[Michael Faraday]] in 1834, from the Greek *ienai*, meaning to go. [[Svante Arrhenius|Svante Arrhenius]] proposed in his 1884 dissertation that [[Salt (chemistry)|salts]] split into charged particles when dissolved, and he won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work.

Elongated bay of the [[Mediterranean Sea]] south of the [[Adriatic Sea]]. It is bounded by southern Italy, including Calabria and Sicily, to the west; southern Albania to the north; and the west coast of [[Greece]], including the Peloponnese, to the east. The main islands, the Ionian Islands, belong to Greece and include Corfu, Kefalonia, Zakynthos, Lefkada and Ithaca. Calypso Deep, the deepest point in the Mediterranean at 5,109 m (16,762 ft), lies in the sea. The sea is one of the most seismically active areas in the world, with frequent [[Earthquake|earthquakes]]. Ancient Greek writers, especially [[Aeschylus|Aeschylus]], linked its name to the myth of Io, who was said to have swum across it. Other legends attribute the name to Ionius, son of Dyrrhachus.

Type of chemical bonding based on electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. It results from the transfer of [[Electron|electrons]] from a [[Metal|metal]] to a [[Nonmetal|nonmetal]], which gives both atoms full valence shells. The metal becomes a positively charged [[Ion|cation]] and the nonmetal a negatively charged anion. Clean transfer never occurs, since all ionic compounds have some covalent character. The term applies when ionic character exceeds covalent character, which requires a large difference in [[Electronegativity|electronegativity]] between the atoms. Ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved but usually not when solid. They generally have high melting points, which rise with the charge of the ions, and they tend to dissolve in [[Water|water]]. The classic example is [[Sodium chloride|sodium chloride]], in which a sodium atom gives its electron to a chlorine atom.

Process by which an atom or molecule acquires a negative or positive charge by gaining or losing [[Electron|electrons]]. The resulting charged particle is an [[Ion|ion]]. Ionization can follow the loss of an electron after collisions with subatomic particles, with other atoms or molecules, or through interaction with [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]]. It can also occur through heterolytic bond cleavage, which produces ion pairs, and in radioactive decay, when an excited nucleus transfers its energy to an inner-shell electron that is ejected. Thermal, photo, impact and field ionization are among its mechanisms. The energy needed, called the ionization energy, varies by element and electron shell. Ionization is central to plasma physics, [[Aurora|auroral]] phenomena and [[Mass spectrometry|mass spectrometry]], a technique in analytical chemistry for identifying molecules.

Subatomic particles or electromagnetic waves with enough energy to ionize atoms or molecules. Ionizing radiation starts around 10 [[Electronvolt|electronvolts]] (eV). [[Gamma ray|Gamma rays]], [[X-ray|X-rays]] and the higher-energy part of the [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] spectrum are ionizing, while lower-energy ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves and radio waves are not. Ionizing particles include alpha particles, beta particles and neutrons, which radioactive decay produces. [[Cosmic ray|Cosmic rays]] and radioactive decay are the main natural sources, and artificial sources include X-ray tubes, particle accelerators and nuclear fission. Because human senses cannot detect it, instruments such as Geiger counters measure it. High acute doses cause radiation burns and [[Acute radiation syndrome|radiation sickness]], while lower doses over long periods can cause cancer. Used in medicine, nuclear power and industry, it is a health hazard without proper measures against excessive exposure. The International Commission on Radiological Protection issues guidance on protection.

Landlocked state in the Upper Midwest of the [[United States|U.S.]] Its capital and largest city is [[Des Moines, Iowa|Des Moines]]. The [[Mississippi River]] forms its eastern border and the [[Missouri River]] much of its western border. In the 18th and early 19th centuries it was part of French and Spanish Louisiana, and its state flag is patterned after the [[Flag of France|flag of France]]. After the [[Louisiana Purchase]], pioneers built an agricultural economy in the Corn Belt, which later diversified into manufacturing, financial services and information technology. The state is known for the Iowa Caucuses, an influential event in national politics.

Class of fast battleships of the U.S. Navy. Six were ordered in 1939 and 1940, but only four, *Iowa*, *New Jersey*, *Missouri* and *Wisconsin*, were completed. In World War II they mainly escorted [[Aircraft carrier|aircraft carriers]] and shelled Japanese positions. During the [[Korean War|Korean War]] they provided naval gunfire support, and in 1968 *New Jersey* shelled Viet Cong forces in the [[Vietnam War|Vietnam War]]. Reactivated and armed with missiles in the 1980s, *Missouri* and *Wisconsin* fired missiles and 16-inch guns at Iraqi targets during Operation Desert Storm in 1991. All four were later donated to nonprofit organizations and became museum ships.

Political scandal in the United States over secret arms sales to [[Iran|Iran]], 1981–86. Reagan administration officials sold arms hoping to free American hostages held in [[Lebanon|Lebanon]] by [[Hezbollah|Hezbollah]], and diverted the profits to the Contras, rebels in [[Nicaragua|Nicaragua]], despite congressional bans. The scandal broke in November 1986. [[Ronald Reagan|Ronald Reagan]] said the U.S. had not traded arms for hostages, then in March 1987 took full responsibility. Investigations found no evidence that Reagan knew the full extent of the programs. Eleven convictions resulted, some later vacated, and most other defendants were pardoned at the end of [[George H. W. Bush|George H. W. Bush]]'s presidency.

Armed conflict between Iran and Iraq, 1980–88. Iraq invaded Iran in September 1980. The Iraqi government, led by [[Saddam Hussein|Saddam Hussein]], aimed to stop [[Ruhollah Khomeini|Ruhollah Khomeini]], Iran's leader after the [[Iranian Revolution|Iranian Revolution]], from exporting Iran's ideology, and to replace Iran as the main power in the [[Persian Gulf|Persian Gulf]]. The war involved large-scale trench warfare and deliberate attacks on civilians, including Iraqi chemical attacks. Iraq's invasion stalled by December 1980, and Iran recaptured its territory by June 1982 before invading Iraq. Under [[United Nations Security Council|United Nations Security Council]] Resolution 598, both countries accepted a ceasefire effective in August 1988. The war caused around 500,000 deaths, the deadliest conventional war between regular armies of developing countries. It made no permanent border changes, and neither country received reparations.

Occupation of the U.S. embassy in Tehran, 1979–81. Militants who seized the embassy on November 4, 1979, took 66 Americans hostage, and 52 were held until January 20, 1981. Backed by [[Ruhollah Khomeini|Ruhollah Khomeini]], they demanded the extradition of [[Mohammad Reza Pahlavi|Mohammad Reza Pahlavi]], the former *shah*, whom the Carter administration had granted asylum for cancer treatment. A U.S. rescue attempt, Operation Eagle Claw, failed in April 1980. The hostages were released one day after the Algiers Accords were signed. The crisis was seen as a major factor in the defeat of [[Jimmy Carter|Jimmy Carter]] in the 1980 presidential election.

Uprising against the monarchy of [[Mohammad Reza Pahlavi|Pahlavi]] in Iran, 1978–79. It replaced the Imperial State of Iran with an Islamic republic led by [[Ruhollah Khomeini|Ruhollah Khomeini]], an Islamist cleric who became supreme leader. The [[1953 Iranian coup d'état|1953 coup]], backed by the CIA and MI6, had overthrown Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh and restored Pahlavi as an absolute monarch. Anti-government demonstrations began in October 1977 and became a broad-based uprising by the end of 1978. Pahlavi left Iran in January 1979. Khomeini returned on February 1, 1979, and the monarchy fell within days. In a March referendum, 98% approved an Islamic republic. Some analysts note that the revolution lacked the usual causes, such as defeat in war or financial crisis. Afterward, Iran supported Shia political movements across the region and declared the destruction of [[Israel|Israel]] a core objective.

Architecture of [[Iran|Iran]] and parts of [[West Asia|West Asia]], the [[Caucasus|Caucasus]] and [[Central Asia|Central Asia]]. Its history dates back to at least 5000 BC, with examples from Turkey and Iraq to Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. Buildings range from vernacular structures to monumental complexes, including gates, palaces and mosques. Rapid growth in cities such as [[Tehran|Tehran]] has brought demolition and new construction. The American historian and archaeologist Arthur Pope held that architecture has always been Iran's supreme art, in both the pre-Islamic and Islamic periods. Without sudden innovations, it developed a recognizable style distinct from the rest of the Muslim world, marked by a feeling for form and scale, structural inventiveness in vault and [[Dome|dome]] construction, and decoration.

Branch of the Indo-Iranian languages within the Indo-European family. Iranian languages, or Iranic languages, are spoken natively by Iranian peoples, mainly on the [[Iranian plateau|Iranian plateau]]. They fall into three stages: Old Iranian, until 400 BCE; Middle Iranian, from 400 BCE to 900 CE; and New Iranian, since 900 CE. The two directly attested Old Iranian languages are Old Persian, from the [[Achaemenid Empire|Achaemenid Empire]], and Avestan, the language of the [[Avesta|Avesta]]. Among the Middle Iranian languages, the best understood are Middle Persian, from the [[Sasanian Empire|Sasanian Empire]]; Parthian, from the [[Parthian Empire|Parthian Empire]]; and Bactrian, from the Kushan and Hephthalite empires.
